1:
The particle matters, and Ellicott presses it: but the Spirit, in strong contrast to the mystery of redemption just celebrated, set against men busying themselves with a mock devotion which dreams God's mercy is purchased by abstinence from meats, or by an unnatural renunciation of home and family. Henry makes the same join from the other side: the previous chapter closed with the mystery of godliness, so this one very fitly opens with the mystery of iniquity. Where the Spirit speaks from is less settled. Gill weighs Daniel's little horn, Christ's warning of false prophets, and Agabus, then settles on Paul speaking now, since the words are plain and stand nowhere else in this form. Wesley points instead to Paul's earlier word to the Thessalonians, and Barnes reads that parallel as showing the truth had already been preached there. Robertson declines to choose between an Old Testament prophecy and a Christian utterance. Ellicott sets it among the supernatural intimations granted to the first generation and rarely after, and takes this for one made to Paul himself. Cyril of Jerusalem uses the verse for another purpose, as standing proof that the Holy Ghost subsists, lives, speaks and foretells.

On expressly nobody dissents: the adverb stands here alone in the New Testament, and Barnes catches its force — in express words, not by hints and symbols and shadowy images. Henry draws an inference the others do not, that the Spirit must therefore be God, since events depending on the tempers and lusts of men could not otherwise be foreseen; and the plainness is what separates this from the heathen oracles, always doubtful. Over the extent of the falling away the room divides. Henry takes comfort in the word: some, not all, for in the worst of times God will have a remnant according to the election of grace. Wesley reads the same word the opposite way — some, yea, many, and by degrees the far greater part — and Barnes agrees it does not imply a small number. Clarke maps two roads in: a man may hold every truth of Christianity and render them of none effect by other doctrines that counteract them, or may deny one essential doctrine while bringing in nothing heterodox. Robertson insists that what is departed from is not creed but faith in God through Christ. Calvin alone predicates the falling away of hearers rather than teachers, since teachers are named in the next clause, and finds it the more damaging that impostors never want disciples.

Chrysostom supplies the image: those who hold the faith are fixed on a safe anchor, while those who fall from it can nowhere rest, and are borne at last into the very gulf of perdition. He names the Manichaeans, the Encratites and the Marcionites, and denies that the prophecy can concern the Jews, to whom neither the latter times nor a departure from the faith applies. The last clause divides the room. Ellicott refuses to let the seducing spirits be watered down into false teachers: they are evil powers subject to Satan, and the doctrines are suggested by them. Clarke prefers the reading of many manuscripts and the chief fathers, spirits of deceit, as more emphatic. Barnes concedes the genitive is ambiguous, and reasons that since the previous clause already says by demons, this one must mean about them; he then lands the whole prophecy on Rome, on the invocation of saints and of the Virgin, the decree of Trent, and the surviving rite of exorcism. Henry reaches the same target by a shorter road, calling the worship of saints and angels as a middle order of deities paganism revived. Calvin agrees on the target but relocates the offence: the controversy is not about flesh or fish, or about Friday or Wednesday, but about men who assume dominion over consciences and forbid what God has permitted.
2:
Every voice here corrects the Authorised construction the same way. The sense is not that demons speak lies in hypocrisy, but that men depart from the faith through the hypocrisy of men that speak lies. Barnes gives two reasons: the Greek word order would have to be inverted to yield the other sense, and that construction, once adopted, must be carried through the whole sentence, so that demons would be the ones forbidding marriage and commanding abstinence from meats. The consequence he draws is the important one — the characteristics that follow belong to the teachers and not to the taught, to the ministry rather than to the body of the people, so that the great apostasy comes about under a hypocritical and arbitrary ministry teaching its own doctrines in place of the divine commands. Robertson adds that the compound for lying speech occurs here alone in the New Testament, a good classical word, Parry says, for liars on a large scale.

On what the lies are the room parts. Gill points at the Romish priests and their doctrines of merit, purgatory, invocation of saints, fastings and pilgrimages, with the fabulous legends and lying wonders, all under a show of godliness. Barnes presses the same identification further and turns to the harder question, whether it is done hypocritically, arguing that learned men in that communion must know the pretended miracles to be tricks, and supporting it with private testimony: a gentleman of high authority told him that in France and Italy young men enter the ministry sincerely, learn in the course of their studies what the system rests on, and by then are committed past retreat. Clarke works by document instead, quoting Edward I's letter of 1305 asking Pope Clement V to canonise a bishop of Hereford because the blind saw and the lame walked by his merits, and disposing of Becket with the remark that since he works no miracles now we may be sure he never worked any. Ellicott declines the whole application. For him the lies are the teaching that it pleases the Creator for men to avoid certain meats and abstain from marriage, the hypocrisy is a mask of holiness got from that asceticism, and the root is wild Oriental speculation about the evil nature of matter.

The last clause divides on one word. Barnes and Wesley take the searing as cauterisation, which destroys feeling: the burnt part becomes rigid and dead to sensibility, and the conscience answering to it will practise fraud without wincing and scourge or burn the innocent without compassion. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson take it instead as branding, which leaves a mark. Ellicott renders it branded in their own conscience as with a hot iron and draws the image from the mark burnt into slaves and criminals; Clarke observes that these men bear their hypocrisy as indelibly in conscience before God as the cauterised bear their crimes in the body before men, and that the heathen supposed the marks legible in the other world. Robertson notes the verb stands here and once in Strabo and nowhere else, and that these men carry the brand of Satan as Paul carried the marks of Christ. Clarke closes with Claudian's Rhadamanthus turning on Rufinus: thou fool, why deny what is manifest, when the deep-burnt marks deform thy conscience and the crimes cannot hide themselves.
3:
The two marks of the apostasy are named, and the room immediately disputes whom they fit. Robertson and Ellicott look east and back: the Essenes, the Therapeutae and other oriental sects had already made abstinence from marriage meritorious, and Ellicott expects the counsel to harden into the dogma of the great Gnostic schools, with Robertson pointing to the Colossian warning against exactly such ascetic practice and observing that Paul nowhere condemns marriage. Gill will not have it. He names the Encratites, Montanists and Manichees only to set them aside, since what the text describes is forbidding in an authoritative way, and that is the Papists forbidding it to their priests under a pretence of purity while allowing them every uncleanness. Wesley says the same in six words, priests, monks and nuns. Clarke allows the Essenes held the sentiment but presses the vow of continency. Barnes agrees with Gill on the target and supplies the document, the tenth canon of Trent on marriage, which pronounces accursed whoever shall say that the married state is to be preferred to virginity; he grants in passing that the words might fit the Essenes, as Koppe supposed, or Judaizing teachers, but holds they fit Rome better.

Ellicott alone asks why the two prohibitions get such unequal treatment, celibacy dismissed in a sentence and food discussed at length. His answer is that the counsel against marriage is so plainly contrary to the scheme of creation that ordinary sense would consign it to obscurity, whereas abstinence from meats could be argued out of the Mosaic restrictions, rightly or wrongly understood, and so threatened to become a controverted question between the Gentile congregations and the Jewish; Paul therefore lifted it at once to higher ground, all food being from the hand of one Maker. Barnes takes the opposite path and stays with particulars, noting that the word covers whatever is eaten but is probably narrowed here to flesh, then quoting a catechism on fast-days and days of abstinence, and the ten-year dispensation granted from 1833 for Saturday. Cyril of Jerusalem, who fasts himself, is the one voice that separates the practice from the error condemned: we abstain from wine and flesh not because we abhor them as abominations but because we look for our reward, and therefore despise not them that eat, nor blame those who take a little wine for the stomach's sake.

The ground of the answer is creation itself: to call anything created unclean, says Ellicott, is an insult to the Creator, and the fact that God made it is enough. Barnes will not let the sentence run loose. Good means good in its place and for the end intended, not good for every use to which it can be put; rye and Indian corn are good, but a man who distils a poisonous liquid out of them and then pleads that every creature of God is good has stopped talking about what God made, and the verse must not be pressed into the service of strong drink. Clarke hears a proverb behind it and cites the heathen form, that the gifts which come from Jove are not to be despised. On the sanctifying, Clarke and Robertson locate the word of God in the grant of Genesis, food set apart to that use by the command itself, Robertson calling the phrase almost a hendiadys, the use of Scripture in prayer. Ellicott presses past the grace before meat, which he says too often degenerates into heartless lip-service or is treated as a charm, to the habit of referring everything to the giver; Wesley notes that Jews and even heathens consecrated the table, and Clarke that those who never thank God for their food are unworthy of the breath they breathe.
6:
What Timothy is to put the brethren in mind of is not agreed. Gill offers a choice between everything laid down in the preceding chapters and the prophecy just delivered; Ellicott narrows it to the ascetic practices, since not a few of the Ephesian flock had already been won over; Clarke reads it as a standing warning that the danger is present now, the forewarned being half armed, and notes that Schoettgen would confine the whole prophecy to the Jews while Bishop Newton would not. Henry takes the verb itself for a definition of the office: those are good ministers who do not study to advance new notions but put the brethren in remembrance, as Peter and Jude both did, because we are apt to forget and slow to learn the things of God. He draws two things out of it that nobody else does — that the way for a minister to grow is to teach, since while we teach others we teach ourselves, and that the taught are called brethren and must be treated so, ministers not being lords of God's heritage. Robertson notes the verb means to place under, to suggest, and calls the title a good minister of Christ Jesus a phrase covering one's whole service.

The participle behind nourished up is a present, and Ellicott builds on that: it marks a continuous and permanent process, better rendered ever training thyself, and the education of a minister of Jesus Christ is never to be considered finished. He then says the thing least expected from him, that asceticism is a winning school for ministers precisely because at a comparatively easy price it wins them a great and thoroughly unhealthy power over the souls of those who practise the austerities, and that a good minister must therefore teach a life which all can lead and not a select few. Robertson finds the verb used by Plato of men nourished in the laws and calls the words of the faith the right diet for babes in Christ, then breaks frame to remark that the Bolshevists in Russia are feeding the children on atheism to get rid of God. Barnes turns the clause about attaining into a charge on the young: the word means to follow closely, side by side, and Timothy having followed his early training out to its results, no young man should by neglect or indolence disappoint the reasonable expectations of his friends.

On the fables the identification splits along familiar lines. Gill will take Jewish traditions, or Gnostic speculation about God and angels, or the doctrines just condemned. Barnes restrains the adjective, insisting that profane here does not mean blasphemous but only lacking the character of true religion, and that old wives' is used exactly as we use silly. Robertson derives the rare compound from the word for an old woman and glosses it as the sort of tale old women tell children, like the Gnostic aeons. Ellicott gives the Rabbinic schools their due and their sentence together: a keen investigation of every book and almost every letter, in which the spirit of the writers was lost and a dry formalism about mint and anise remained, with legend grown so thickly round the old history that a student could no longer separate true from false. Clarke agrees about the Talmud and then turns the charge on Rome, setting the Aurea Legenda and Joseline's Life of St. Patrick column for column against it, with miracles more numerous and more stupendous than all the necessary ones wrought by Christ and his apostles. The remedy is a gymnasium. Clarke and Wesley both hear the Greek games in the verb, the training before the contest, except that the chaplet of leaves was corruptible and this crown does not fade; Ellicott insists the piety meant is the practical kind, which leavens the life of the slave as much as the patrician.
8:
Four different things are meant by bodily exercise, depending on who is reading. Wesley takes it flatly and literally — it increases the health and strength of the body, and that is the little profit. Clarke hears the gymnasium still echoing from the previous verse and makes it the Greek games, worth little because they look only to this life and the applause of men. Barnes and Ellicott take it for the austerities of verse three, the abstinence and penance the Essenes made central. Gill canvasses all of these, rejects each, and lands where none of the others go: mere formal external worship, as opposed to spiritual. On little Robertson raises a question Barnes had conceded, whether the phrase means for a little while or for little, and prefers extent, since the next clause answers with for all things. Ellicott then says what one does not expect from the man who has spent three verses attacking asceticism. Such training has in many cases lifted the individual to a higher spiritual state and is in a certain sense profitable; the harm is that the rigid ascetic has stepped off the platform on which ordinary men and women move, so that his thoughts have ceased to be their thoughts; and Paul stops short of entire condemnation of a life which the Sinless One had guardedly commended.

Barnes spends himself on the promise for this life and gives it the widest possible reach: godliness favours health by promoting temperance and frugality, clears the intellect, quiets the conscience, prospers a man in business by making him sober and prudent, earns a good name, and meets him with calmness at his death. Religion, he says, injures no one; it makes no one poorer, prompts to no crime, engenders no disease. He adds that every man privately believes he would be a Christian if he were ever certainly to be happy, and claims that true piety sends nobody to the alms-house, few of whose inmates give any evidence of religion. Ellicott keeps the same promise but changes its direction, making godliness not an inward holiness but an operative piety springing from love of Christ, whose influence is world-wide where the ascetic's is circumscribed, illuminating every rank and age. On the formula that follows, Ellicott hears one of the watchwords already current in the first congregations, drawn now from a hymn and now from a public prayer; Robertson notices the one thing that distinguishes this occurrence from the parallel earlier in the letter, that here the saying points backward to what has just been said rather than forward.

Clarke reads the next verse as a deliberate correction, and says so: it was necessary to explain what had gone before, because Paul did not mean that the followers of God enjoy worldly prosperity and exemption from natural evils. It is precisely because they exercise themselves to godliness that they have labour and reproach. Gill lists what the labour was, not preaching and not their trades but stripes, imprisonment, watchings, hunger, thirst, cold and nakedness; Ellicott has the missionaries shrinking from no shame however agonising, and hears the epithet living set against the dumb idols of the Ephesian temples. Then comes the hard clause: how a man can be Saviour of all and specially of some. Barnes distinguishes two senses, preserver of all from famine and war and peril, and provider of a salvation offered to all, and holds firmly that only believers are actually saved. Robertson borrows White's formula, potentially Saviour of all and actually Saviour of the faithful. Clarke and Wesley press the offer further — all have been purchased, all may believe, and those that perish perish through their own fault. Ellicott spends most of his space repudiating universalism as a perilous theory, and then allows that the atonement may work consequences reaching far beyond the limits of human thought or sober speculation.
11:
Chrysostom takes the two verbs as a working rule and states it sharply: some things must be commanded and others taught, and if you command where teaching is required you become ridiculous, while if you teach where you ought to command you are open to the same reproach. Wickedness is to be forbidden with all authority; parting with possessions, professing virginity and discoursing of faith are matters for teaching. He gives a test case — a man who wears an amulet knowing it wrong needs only a command, but the man who does it ignorantly must be taught his error. Gill applies the distinction to the chapter just closed, commanding rejection of the fables and teaching the profitableness of godliness. Ellicott takes the things to be the meaning of godliness itself, the everyday piety set against a strained asceticism, and says it must enter both the public charge and the private teaching. Barnes uses the verse to press the point he has just made: a minister is as solemnly bound to teach that there is a sense in which God is the Saviour of all men as he is to teach that only believers are saved. Clarke reduces it to a preaching programme: religion is profitable for both worlds, and Christ tasted death for every man.

The next clause is read two ways. Barnes, Wesley, Henry and Clarke take it as a charge to give no occasion — do not act so that any shall despise you, since youth is not despised where vanities and follies are avoided, and boyish playfulness ill becomes a minister at any age. Chrysostom and Gill hear an instruction to exert authority instead, and Chrysostom draws the line that makes the difference workable: contempt offered to himself a teacher ought to bear, for teaching is commended by longsuffering, but where the salvation of others is at stake forbearance is not meekness but coldness, and he must interpose with authority. Gill guesses Timothy at about twenty-three, noting that Saul was called a young man at thirty. Ellicott puts him at not more than forty and goes where nobody else goes: this warning, with the note about his stomach and the request at Corinth that no man despise him, suggests there was nothing winning in Timothy's appearance. He generalises it — beauty was the exception among the early leaders, Paul himself mean and insignificant in Luther's phrase, and Tertullian, Clement and Justin all describing Christ as having no human beauty, Origen alone dissenting — and concludes that this religion was meant to owe nothing to the ordinary conditions of human success.

The six graces are then disputed almost item by item. On the first, Barnes insists it is not public teaching but familiar conversation, Ellicott and Robertson take it as both, and Clarke alone makes it doctrine, nothing but the truth of God, because nothing else saves souls. On the second, Ellicott and Robertson agree the old rendering misleads and the word means manner of life. The third is the interesting one: Clarke reports it missing from the chief manuscripts and from the Syriac, Vulgate and Itala, that Griesbach leaves it out and a later hand probably added it, and Ellicott concurs that it is in none of the older authorities — while Wesley and Barnes, undisturbed, gloss it as the whole temper and the government of the passions. On faith, Clarke and Wesley agree it means fidelity rather than belief, since it stands among other graces and doctrine has been named already; Ellicott pairs it with love as faith towards God. On purity, Robertson notes the word is used of a Nazirite, Clarke passes on the advice of a holy minister to converse sparingly with women, and Barnes turns savage, denying that it enjoins celibacy and declaring that if the apostle had wished to corrupt the church he would have enjoined celibacy on the clergy.
13:
Robertson opens with a correction nobody else notices: the Greek is a present indicative, so the sense is while I am coming rather than till I come. Gill supplies what happened: Paul hoped to be at Ephesus shortly, was prevented, and afterwards sent for its elders to meet him at Miletus. On the reading the room divides by degrees. Ellicott is certain it is the public reading of Scripture in the congregation, borrowed from the synagogue, and then asks the question the passage invites: were any books read there besides the Old Testament? He will not answer certainly, but thinks it probable that one of the older Gospels, most likely Mark, was already in use, and points to Justin's account of Christian worship as showing how soon that became regular. Barnes leans the other way and takes it of private reading, a perusal of whatever would qualify Timothy for his public work, chiefly the Old Testament but not only, since Paul himself shows acquaintance with the Greek poets. Clarke and Robertson will have both, Clarke reasoning that reading at home is what makes a man fit to expound in the assembly. Wesley says both and turns on his own wing: enthusiasts, observe this, expect no end without the means.

Clarke uses the clause to draw up a reading list for his own century, arguing that in the apostles' day the preacher's business was to state the great facts and prove them, whereas now the truth must be defended and obsolete customs explained from ancient writers. Hebrew and Greek come first, Latin next — worth the trouble if only for Jerome, whose commentary he calls in many respects erroneous and superficial — then Arabic and Syriac, the latter being in effect the language Christ and the apostles spoke in Judea. He then withdraws the pressure, granting that none of this is absolutely necessary, since there are many eminent ministers without such advantages. On the two words that follow, Ellicott separates them by faculty, exhortation addressed to the feelings and teaching to the understanding, with exposition and even dogmatic instruction included in the second. Robertson notices the order and doubts it: exhortation is not meant to precede instruction but to follow it in actual public work, since exhortation needs teaching to rest upon, which he offers as a hint for preachers today.

What the gift is, and what conveyed it, divides the room again. Gill excludes natural ability, learning and even saving grace, and defines it as a peculiar gift of interpreting Scripture, a treasure in an earthen vessel not to be wrapped in a napkin. Clarke says plainly that it was the gifts and graces of the Spirit received at the imposition of hands, and warns that unimproved they would be withdrawn by the Head of the church. Barnes denies exactly this. Having traced the word through the New Testament, he concludes that no mysterious influence was conveyed by the act and no new grace infused, and that the gift is the whole train of circumstances by which Timothy came to be qualified. Barnes deflates the prophecy too, making it the predictions and hopes of pious friends who had observed his fitness, where Ellicott has an inspired prophet declaring the divine intention and Wesley an immediate direction from God; Robertson settles it grammatically, accompanied by prophecy and not bestowed by it. Then the presbytery. Barnes finds here the decisive proof of his own polity: more than one man laid on hands, the power came from the whole body, and no ordination in the New Testament was performed by one man alone — a Presbyterian would describe an ordination in exactly these words and an Episcopalian would not. Wesley reads the same verse as Paul's own act with the elders joining in the solemnity, and Robertson quietly removes the ground under Barnes by observing that the preposition marks accompaniment, not instrument.
15:
Ellicott and Robertson agree the familiar rendering is too contemplative: the verb means be diligent in these things, keep on practising them. Wesley refuses the correction, holding that Scripture makes no distinction between meditating and contemplating whatever others do, and that true meditation is faith, hope, love and joy melted down together by the fire of the Spirit and offered up in secret. Gill wants both, and gives the reading its own image, the Scriptures laboriously searched as men dig in mines for silver ore, obscure passages compared with plain. On the next clause Barnes and Clarke reach independently for the same tag from Horace, that a man may be wholly in one thing, and Robertson finds Plutarch saying it of Caesar and translates it up to his ears in work. Barnes then lists what a minister must not live for — money, fame, pleasure, literature or science pursued for their own sakes, the reputation of an elegant scholar or an accomplished gentleman — and generalises past the ministry: the man who has one great purpose to which he makes everything else bend will rise, and the man who has not can expect to accomplish nothing.

Clarke and Wesley then say the same thing twice over. Clarke quotes Bengel by name and in Latin against the minister who consumes a principal part of his life in worldly company, foreign studies, and collecting books, shells and coins, adding that such men often know nothing of the use of their collections, only seeing them and showing them, and should be prayed for and pitied unless the whole is formed to illustrate the sacred records. Wesley gives the same judgment without the citation: he that is wholly in these will be little in worldly company, in other studies, in collecting books, medals or butterflies, wherein many pastors drone away so considerable a part of their lives. On the profiting, Barnes prefers the marginal in all things and observes that real progress will be seen by others, and the want of it understood just as well. Ellicott turns the same word into a rule against standing still, no resting content with knowledge acquired and no satisfaction with the present spiritual life, and Robertson, deriving it from cutting a way forward, adds that it is inspiring to watch a young preacher grow, since the church grows with him.

The last charge is two halves that cannot be separated, and Ellicott states the reciprocity: without true teaching the pure life of a pastor will fail to win souls, and the most efficient instruction is worthless unless the life corresponds. Gill extends the first half to a minister's gifts, the errors abroad, and his flock, which he calls the other part of himself. Barnes extends it to health, temper, habits and manners, and delivers the sentence he is remembered for: there is no religion in a filthy person, in uncouth manners, in bad grammar or slovenly habits, and to be a real gentleman should be as much a matter of conscience with a minister as to be a real Christian. Robertson sees the ditch on both sides — some young preachers are careless of their health and habits, and some are too finical. Clarke warns what follows neglect: the divine influence recedes, and like Samson shorn the man becomes as any other, unable to make others feel what he no longer feels. On saving himself and his hearers, Barnes denies any merit in the labour while insisting that an unfaithful minister cannot be saved, and closes on a single soul rescued as a brighter gem than ever sparkled on the brow of royalty. Clarke closes otherwise. Having spent the chapter pointing at Rome, and having reproduced Bishop Newton's whole dissertation, he declines to conclude: which mode of interpretation is best he will not say, and whether God had that church alone in view he dare not affirm.
